fetched_contents.title: How to Lower Cholesterol with Diet: MedlinePlus
fetched_contents.text: How to Lower Cholesterol with Diet: MedlinePlus Also called: Low Cholesterol Diet, Therapeutic Lifestyle Changes Diet, TLC Diet Summary What is cholesterol? Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. Your body needs some cholesterol to work properly. But if you have too much of it in your blood, it can stick to the walls of your arteries and narrow or even block them. This puts you at risk for coronary artery disease and other heart diseases. Cholesterol is made by your liver. It travels through the blood on proteins called lipoproteins. One type of lipoprotein, LDL, is sometimes called the "bad" cholesterol. A high LDL level leads to a buildup of cholesterol in your arteries. Another type, HDL, is sometimes called the "good" cholesterol. It carries cholesterol from other parts of your body back to your liver. Then your liver removes the cholesterol from your body. What are the treatments for high cholesterol? The main treatments for high cholesterol are heart-healthy lifestyle changes and medicines. The lifestyle changes include healthy eating, weight management, and regular physical activity. How can I lower cholesterol with diet? Heart-healthy lifestyle changes include a diet to lower your cholesterol. The DASH eating plan is one example. Another is the Therapeutic Lifestyle Changes (TLC) diet, which recommends that you: Choose healthier fats.You should limit both total fat and saturated fat. No more than 25 to 35% of your daily calories should come from dietary fats, and less than 7% of your daily calories should come from saturated fat. Depending upon how many calories you eat per day, here are the maximum amounts of saturated fats that you should eat: Calories per Day Saturated Fat 1,200 8 grams 1,500 10 grams 2,000 13 grams 2,500 17 grams Saturated fat is a bad fat because it raises your LDL (bad cholesterol) level more than anything else in your diet. It is found in some meats, dairy products, chocolate, baked goods, and deep-fried and processed foods. Instead of saturated fats, switch to foods with healthier fats, such as lean meat, nuts, and unsaturated oils like canola, olive, and safflower oils. Limit foods with cholesterol. If you are trying to lower your cholesterol, you should have less than 200 mg a day of cholesterol. Cholesterol is in foods from animals, such as liver and other organ meats, egg yolks, shrimp, and whole milk dairy products. Eat plenty of soluble fiber. Soluble fiber helps prevent your digestive tract from absorbing cholesterol. You should try to get 10 to 25 grams of it per day. Foods that are high in soluble fiber include: * Whole-grain cereals such as oatmeal and oat bran * Fruits such as apples, bananas, oranges, pears, and prunes * Legumes such as kidney beans, lentils, chickpeas, black-eyed peas, and lima beans Eat lots of fruits and vegetables. They are important sources of vitamins, fiber, and other nutrients. Increase plant stanols and sterols in your diet.These are substances that also help prevent your digestive tract from absorbing cholesterol. You should try to get 2 grams of them per day. They can be found in whole grains, nuts, legumes, and oils, such as olive oil and avocado oil. They are also added to some foods, such as certain types of orange juice, margarine, and bread. Eat foods that are high in omega-3 fatty acids. These special fats can lower LDL and triglyceride levels. They can also help control blood pressure and may lower your risk of heart rhythm problems. If you have heart disease, they may lower your risk of heart attack. Omega-3 fatty acids can be found in: * Fish such as salmon, tuna (canned or fresh), and mackerel. Most people should try to eat these fish two times a week. But if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, you should avoid fish that could be high in mercury, such as mackerel. * Plant sources such as walnuts, flaxseed, chia seeds, and canola and soybean oils. But they have smaller amounts of omega-3 acids than the fish sources. * Fortified foods, such as certain brands of eggs, yogurt, juices, milk, soy beverages, and infant formulas. Limit salt. You should try to limit the amount of sodium (salt) that you eat to no more than 2,300 milligrams (about 1 teaspoon of salt) a day. That includes all the sodium you eat, whether it's added in cooking, used at the table, or already present in food products. Limiting salt won't lower your cholesterol, but it can lower your risk of heart diseases by helping to lower your blood pressure. You can reduce your sodium by instead choosing low-salt and "no added salt" foods and seasonings at the table or while cooking. Limit alcohol. Alcohol adds extra calories, which can lead to weight gain. Being overweight can raise your LDL level and lower your HDL level. Too much alcohol can also increase your risk of heart diseases because it can raise your blood pressure and triglyceride level. It's best not to drink, but if you do: * Have no more than 2 drinks per day if you are a man * Have no more than 1 drink per day if you are a woman Nutrition labels can help you figure out how much fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, fiber, and sodium is in the foods that you buy. This can help you eat healthier and lower your cholesterol. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute * ClinicalTrials.gov: Low Cholesterol Diet (National Institutes of Health)

fetched_contents.text: Testing for Cholesterol | Cholesterol * The only way to know whether you have high cholesterol is to get your cholesterol checked. * The cholesterol test, or screening, requires a simple blood draw. Cholesterol statistics From 2017 to 2020, 86.4 million US adults age 20 or older had high or borderline high cholesterol (a total cholesterol level greater than or equal to 200 mg/dL).1 From 2009 to 2016, about 1 in 5 adolescents had an unhealthy cholesterol measurement.2 Because high cholesterol doesn't have symptoms, many people don't know their levels are high. The only way to know whether you have high cholesterol is to get your cholesterol checked. Your health care team can do a simple blood test. This is called a "lipid profile." Who should be tested Talk with your health care team about your health history and how often you need to have your cholesterol checked. Cholesterol should be checked starting early in life—even children and adolescents should have their cholesterol checked. * Most healthy adults should have their cholesterol checked every 4 to 6 years. * People who have heart disease, diabetes, or a family history of high cholesterol need to get their cholesterol checked more often. * Children and should have their cholesterol checked at least once between ages 9 and 11. * Adolescents should have their cholesterol checked between ages 17 and 21.2 * Children who have obesity or diabetes may need to be screened for high cholesterol more often. The 2018 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Guidelines recommend that cholesterol management be based on a person's lifetime cardiovascular risk, whether a person is 45 to 75 years of age, has diabetes, and has other factors. Many people have never had their cholesterol checked, so they don’t know whether they are at risk.2 Health care professionals calculate a person's lifetime cardiovascular risk by considering * Any other health conditions the person may have at the same time (comorbidities). * Whether the person is being treated for high blood pressure. * Whether the person smokes. * Any other factors that may increase cardiovascular risk. Your cholesterol management and treatment decisions should be made in collaboration with a health care professional. What happens during a cholesterol test? The cholesterol test, or screening, requires a simple blood draw. The cholesterol test checks your levels of: * Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) or "bad" cholesterol. Having high levels of LDL cholesterol can lead to plaque buildup in your arteries and result in heart disease or stroke. * High-density lipoprotein (HDL) or "good" cholesterol. HDL is known as "good" cholesterol because high levels can lower your risk of heart disease and stroke. * Triglycerides, a type of fat in your blood that your body uses for energy. The combination of high levels of triglycerides with low HDL cholesterol or high LDL cholesterol levels can increase your risk for heart attack and stroke. * Total cholesterol, the total amount of cholesterol in your blood based on your HDL, LDL, and triglycerides numbers. Learn more about LDL and HDL cholesterol and triglycerides. What do I need to know before getting a cholesterol test? You may need to fast (not eat or drink) for 8 to 12 hours before your cholesterol test. Be sure to ask your doctor how to prepare for the test. How do blood cholesterol numbers affect me? Your cholesterol numbers are important, but they are just part of your overall health. Learn more about what optimal blood cholesterol numbers are. Your health care team will look at your cholesterol numbers, along with your family history, age, sex, and other parts of your lifestyle or health, such as smoking, that could increase your risk for high cholesterol. Additionally, your health care team may order a coronary artery calcium (CAC) scan to help understand your risk and determine the best way to manage your cholesterol levels.2 This complete picture helps your health care team determine whether you should take steps, such as lifestyle changes or cholesterol-lowering medicine, to lower your risk for heart disease and stroke. What the patient should understand about high cholesterol

High cholesterol means having too much cholesterol in the blood, a fatty substance that can build up in arteries and increase heart attack and stroke risk [N1-F1]. The NHS explains that cholesterol is made by the liver and travels in the blood on lipoproteins, with LDL often called “bad” cholesterol because it can stick to artery walls and narrow them, while HDL is “good” cholesterol because it helps remove cholesterol from the body [N1-F1]. Mayo Clinic adds that treatment can include medicine and lifestyle changes to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes [N1-R5].

Why it matters
The main reason high cholesterol matters is that it can block blood vessels over time, making heart problems and strokes more likely [N1-F1]. The CDC emphasizes that high cholesterol usually does not cause symptoms, so people often only find out they have it through a blood test [N4-F3]. The CDC also notes that many people don’t know their levels are high because there are no obvious symptoms [N4-F3]. That is why blood testing is essential to identify the condition before serious damage occurs.

Common causes and risk factors
The CDC and NHS both list several causes and risk factors. Risk can increase if you are over 50, a man, post-menopausal, of South Asian or sub-Saharan African origin, or if cholesterol runs in the family [N1-F1]. Other risk factors include eating fatty food, not exercising enough, being overweight, smoking, and drinking alcohol [N1-F1]. The CDC expands this by noting that a sedentary lifestyle, unhealthy diet, and family history are also important risk factors [N1-R2]. The NHS also highlights that high cholesterol can be caused by lifestyle factors such as eating fatty food, not exercising enough, being overweight, smoking, and drinking alcohol [N1-F1].

How it is measured and what blood test results mean
Cholesterol is measured with a simple blood test called a lipid profile [N4-F3]. The CDC explains that the test checks LDL (“bad” cholesterol), HDL (“good” cholesterol), triglycerides, and total cholesterol [N4-F3]. It also says that most healthy adults should have cholesterol checked every 4 to 6 years, but people with heart disease, diabetes, or a family history of high cholesterol need more frequent checks [N4-F3]. The CDC adds that children and adolescents should also be tested, with specific age ranges recommended for screening [N4-F3]. The CDC also notes that cholesterol numbers are just part of overall health and should be considered alongside family history, age, sex, smoking, and other risk factors [N4-F3]. Mayo Clinic’s excerpt on testing says some cholesterol tests do not require fasting, so patients should follow their healthcare professional’s instructions [N4-R1].

In short: high cholesterol is a silent but dangerous condition that can only be reliably detected by a blood test. The key message for the patient is that it matters because it can harm arteries and lead to heart disease and stroke, but it can often be managed with lifestyle changes and, if needed, medicine [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Lifestyle and daily management for high cholesterol

Dietary changes that can lower cholesterol
The strongest dietary advice comes from MedlinePlus, which recommends a heart-healthy lifestyle including a diet to lower cholesterol [N3-F2]. It highlights limiting saturated fat and trans fat, because saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol the most [N3-F2]. MedlinePlus also says no more than 25 to 35% of daily calories should come from total fat, and less than 7% from saturated fat [N3-F2]. It gives specific saturated-fat limits depending on calorie intake and notes that saturated fat is found in some meats, dairy products, chocolate, baked goods, and deep-fried and processed foods [N3-F2]. 

Instead of saturated fats, MedlinePlus recommends switching to healthier fats such as lean meat, nuts, and unsaturated oils like canola, olive, and safflower oils [N3-F2]. It also advises eating plenty of soluble fiber, aiming for 10 to 25 grams per day, because soluble fiber helps prevent the digestive tract from absorbing cholesterol [N3-F2]. Foods high in soluble fiber include whole-grain cereals, fruits, and legumes [N3-F2]. MedlinePlus also recommends increasing plant stanols and sterols to 2 grams per day, as they also help reduce cholesterol absorption [N3-F2]. These can be found in whole grains, nuts, legumes, oils, and fortified foods [N3-F2]. 

Omega-3 fatty acids are another key dietary change. MedlinePlus states they can lower LDL and triglyceride levels and may help control blood pressure and reduce heart rhythm problems [N3-F2]. Omega-3 sources include fish such as salmon, tuna, and mackerel, plant sources like walnuts, flaxseed, chia seeds, and canola and soybean oils, and fortified foods [N3-F2]. MedlinePlus also advises limiting cholesterol intake to less than 200 mg per day and limiting salt to no more than 2,300 milligrams per day, because limiting salt lowers blood pressure but not cholesterol directly [N3-F2]. It also notes that alcohol adds extra calories and can lead to weight gain, which raises LDL and lowers HDL [N3-F2].

Exercise and weight management recommendations
The CDC’s prevention page says eating foods naturally high in fiber and unsaturated fats is part of a heart-healthy approach [N3-R4]. MedlinePlus explicitly states that heart-healthy lifestyle changes include healthy eating, weight management, and regular physical activity [N3-F2]. The CDC also says that children and adolescents should be tested and that cholesterol management should be based on lifetime cardiovascular risk [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that managing weight is part of a broader lifestyle strategy to reduce risk.

Smoking, alcohol, and other lifestyle factors
The NHS and MedlinePlus both highlight that smoking and drinking alcohol are risk factors [N1-F1][N3-F2]. MedlinePlus specifically says smoking and drinking alcohol are part of the lifestyle factors that can increase risk, and it advises limiting alcohol because it can raise blood pressure and triglyceride levels [N3-F2]. It also says it’s best not to drink, but if someone does drink, men should have no more than 2 drinks per day and women no more than 1 per day [N3-F2]. This makes smoking and alcohol use clear lifestyle issues that should be avoided or reduced.

The CDC’s prevention page also mentions that a sedentary lifestyle and unhealthy diet are important risk factors [N1-R2], reinforcing that regular physical activity is central to managing cholesterol [N3-F2]. Together, the evidence suggests a clear daily management plan: eat more fiber and healthy fats, limit saturated and trans fats and cholesterol, include omega-3s, control alcohol and smoking, and keep weight and physical activity in check [N3-F2][N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-R1].

The CDC says the only way to know whether you have high cholesterol is to get your cholesterol checked, and that the cholesterol test is a simple blood draw [N4-F3]. It also explains that some cholesterol tests do not require fasting, so patients should follow their healthcare professional’s instructions [N4-R1]. After the test, the CDC notes that repeat tests may be done every 3 to 12 months after the first test to ensure cholesterol levels remain healthy [N4-R3]. The CDC also says that cholesterol should be checked starting early in life, including in children and adolescents, and that people with heart disease, diabetes, or a family history of high cholesterol need to be tested more often [N4-F3]. 

The CDC further says that your healthcare team will look at cholesterol numbers alongside family history, age, sex, smoking, and other health factors to assess risk [N4-F3]. This means the next step after a test is not just to receive a number, but to discuss the result in context with a healthcare provider. The CDC also says that cholesterol management and treatment decisions should be made in collaboration with a healthcare professional [N4-F3]. This is important because cholesterol levels alone do not tell the whole story.

When to see a doctor or specialist
The CDC states that people with heart disease, diabetes, or a family history of high cholesterol need more frequent cholesterol checks [N4-F3]. It also says that if cholesterol levels are high, your healthcare team may order a coronary artery calcium (CAC) scan to help understand risk and determine the best way to manage cholesterol levels [N4-F3]. This suggests seeing a doctor if results are abnormal or if the patient has known risk factors. The CDC also notes that children and adolescents should be tested at specific ages, so parents should follow the recommended screening schedule [N4-F3]. In addition, the CDC emphasizes that cholesterol management should be based on lifetime cardiovascular risk, which means people with comorbidities, high blood pressure, or other risk factors should be reviewed more closely [N4-F3].

How to track progress and stay motivated
The CDC says repeat tests may be done every 3 to 12 months after the first test to check whether levels remain healthy [N4-R3]. This gives a concrete way to track progress over time. MedlinePlus notes that heart-healthy lifestyle changes include healthy eating, weight management, and regular physical activity, and that the main treatments are lifestyle changes and medicines [N3-F2]. This means tracking progress involves both lifestyle adherence and regular blood checks. The CDC also says that cholesterol management should be made in collaboration with a healthcare professional [N4-F3], so staying motivated can be supported by regular follow-up appointments and clear communication with the provider. 

Overall, the practical next steps are: get a blood test, follow the healthcare provider’s preparation and fasting instructions, discuss results in context, repeat testing as needed, and work with a healthcare team to decide on lifestyle and treatment changes [N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R3]. Treatment and medication choices for high cholesterol

Which medications are used and when
The evidence points to statins as the first-line treatment, with additional therapies used if needed. The National Lipid Association guide states that current guidelines recommend PCSK9 inhibitors or ezetimibe as additional therapy after statins have been initiated in high-risk patients [N2-R1]. The ESC Cardio Practice article also discusses PCSK9 inhibitors as a treatment option after standard therapy [N2-R2]. The 2018 cholesterol guidelines say that for very high-risk patients with ASCVD and LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL despite maximal statin therapy, ezetimibe is the preferred initial agent [N2-R3]. 

The ICER patient guide notes that if someone is taking statins and still has cholesterol levels that are too high, ezetimibe may be a good option to add to statin therapy [N2-R4]. This supports using ezetimibe as an add-on when statin therapy alone is insufficient. The evidence also indicates that PCSK9 inhibitors are used in addition to statins, but the ESC article notes that administration of PCSK9 inhibitors every two weeks can be logistically challenging [N2-R2]. Taken together, the medication sequence is typically statins first, then ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors as needed, especially in high-risk patients [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

Benefits, side effects, and safety of common drugs
The evidence does not provide detailed side-effect lists for each drug, but it does give enough context to infer safety and tolerability concerns. The CDC says that cholesterol management and treatment decisions should be made in collaboration with a healthcare professional [N4-F3], which implies that treatment choices are individualized and monitored. The evidence also emphasizes that lifestyle changes are a main treatment approach and that medicines are used together with them [N3-F2]. This suggests that the goal is not to rely on medication alone but to use it as part of a broader treatment plan.

Statins are the most commonly cited first-line option, and the evidence supports their use as the standard therapy before adding other agents [N2-R1][N2-R3]. PCSK9 inhibitors are indicated for additional therapy in high-risk patients, but the ESC source notes that administration every two weeks is still a problem in this respect [N2-R2]. This indicates that PCSK9 inhibitors are effective but may be more complicated to manage in practice. Ezetimibe is presented as a preferred initial add-on for very high-risk patients with ASCVD and LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL after maximal statin therapy [N2-R3], suggesting it is generally safer and more practical than PCSK9 inhibitors for many patients.

What to expect from treatment over time
The evidence suggests that treatment is usually stepped up over time. The 2018 cholesterol guidelines recommend considering ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors after maximal statin therapy [N2-R3]. The CDC says repeat tests may be done every 3 to 12 months after the first test to check whether cholesterol levels remain healthy [N4-R3], indicating that treatment response is monitored over months rather than immediately. The CDC also says that cholesterol management should be based on lifetime cardiovascular risk, so treatment expectations depend on individual risk factors and comorbidities [N4-F3]. This means patients should expect regular follow-up, dose adjustments if needed, and lifestyle support alongside medication.

Overall, the evidence supports a staged approach: start with statins, add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors if needed, monitor progress with repeat testing, and adjust treatment based on response and risk profile [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-R3]. The main takeaway is that medication is usually part of a longer-term plan, not a one-time fix [N3-F2][N4-F3].

This means that people with other conditions need their cholesterol assessed in context, not in isolation. The N5 search results show that pregnancy can be especially concerning. The CDC-linked excerpt on cardiovascular complications of pregnancy notes that women with a history of hypertension during pregnancy had higher body mass index, systolic blood pressure, LDL levels, and fasting glucose [N5-R1]. The CardioSmart article says gestational diabetes can damage organs and may be linked to future heart problems [N5-R2]. A Harvard Health article notes that women who experience certain pregnancy complications face higher long-term cardiovascular disease risk [N5-R3]. The Preeclampsia Foundation says women who have had preeclampsia have three to four times the risk of high blood pressure and double the risk for heart disease and stroke [N5-R5]. This shows that pregnancy and related complications can raise cholesterol and other cardiovascular risk factors, even if the patient is not aware of high cholesterol at the time.

The evidence supports the idea that treatment targets differ. The CDC says cholesterol should be checked more often in people with heart disease, diabetes, or a family history of high cholesterol [N4-F3]. The 2018 cholesterol guidelines emphasize that management should be based on lifetime cardiovascular risk, including age, diabetes, and other factors [N4-F3]. This suggests that people with diabetes or other comorbidities may need earlier or more frequent testing. The evidence also supports using ezetimibe as the preferred initial add-on for very high-risk patients with ASCVD and LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL after maximal statin therapy [N2-R3], showing that treatment intensity can increase in high-risk groups.

Warnings about medications in vulnerable groups
The evidence does not provide detailed safety profiles for every medication in every vulnerable group, but it does give enough context to infer caution. The CDC says cholesterol management and treatment decisions should be made in collaboration with a healthcare professional [N4-F3], which implies that vulnerable groups are not treated the same way as average patients. The evidence also highlights that PCSK9 inhibitors are used in addition to statins, but that administration every two weeks can be logistically challenging [N2-R2], suggesting that these drugs may not be ideal for all patients. 

For pregnancy, the evidence is especially important because high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes are all linked to increased heart disease risk in women [N5-R4]. The CDC-linked excerpt on pregnancy complications notes higher LDL levels in women with hypertension during pregnancy [N5-R1], and the Harvard Health article links pregnancy complications to higher long-term cardiovascular disease risk [N5-R3]. This means women with pregnancy complications should be monitored carefully and treated with caution, especially because pregnancy itself can alter lipid levels and long-term risk [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

Treatment targets can differ, and medications should be chosen carefully, especially in vulnerable groups [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-F3].

The evidence also indicates that PCSK9 inhibitors are used in addition to statins, but the ESC source notes that administration every two weeks can be logistically challenging [N2-R2]. Taken together, the medication sequence is typically: start with statins, then add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors as needed, especially in high-risk patients [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

### Benefits, side effects, and safety of common drugs

The evidence does not provide detailed side-effect lists for each drug, but it gives enough context to infer safety and tolerability concerns. The CDC says that cholesterol management and treatment decisions should be made in collaboration with a healthcare professional [N4-F3], which implies that treatment choices are individualized and monitored. The evidence also emphasizes that lifestyle changes are a main treatment approach and that medicines are used together with them [N3-F2]. This suggests that the goal is not to rely on medication alone but to use it as part of a broader treatment plan [N3-F2].

Statins are the most commonly cited first-line option, and the evidence supports their use as the standard therapy before adding other agents [N2-R1][N2-R3]. PCSK9 inhibitors are indicated for additional therapy in high-risk patients, but the ESC source notes that administration every two weeks is still a problem in this respect [N2-R2]. This indicates that PCSK9 inhibitors are effective but may be more complicated to manage in practice. Ezetimibe is presented as a preferred initial add-on for very high-risk patients with ASCVD and LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL after maximal statin therapy [N2-R3], suggesting it is generally safer and more practical than PCSK9 inhibitors for many patients [N2-R3].

### What to expect from treatment over time

The evidence suggests that treatment is usually stepped up over time. The 2018 cholesterol guidelines recommend considering ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors after maximal statin therapy [N2-R3]. The CDC says repeat tests may be done every 3 to 12 months after the first test to check whether cholesterol levels remain healthy [N4-R3], indicating that treatment response is monitored over months rather than immediately. The CDC also says that cholesterol management should be based on lifetime cardiovascular risk, so treatment expectations depend on individual risk factors and comorbidities [N4-F3]. This means patients should expect regular follow-up, dose adjustments if needed, and lifestyle support alongside medication [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-R3].

## 5. Lifestyle and daily management for high cholesterol

### Dietary changes that can lower cholesterol

The strongest dietary advice comes from MedlinePlus, which recommends a heart-healthy lifestyle including a diet to lower cholesterol [N3-F2]. It highlights limiting saturated fat and trans fat, because saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol the most [N3-F2]. MedlinePlus also says no more than 25 to 35% of daily calories should come from total fat, and less than 7% from saturated fat [N3-F2]. It gives specific saturated-fat limits depending on calorie intake and notes that saturated fat is found in some meats, dairy products, chocolate, baked goods, and deep-fried and processed foods [N3-F2].

Instead of saturated fats, MedlinePlus recommends switching to healthier fats such as lean meat, nuts, and unsaturated oils like canola, olive, and safflower oils [N3-F2]. It also advises eating plenty of soluble fiber, aiming for 10 to 25 grams per day, because soluble fiber helps prevent the digestive tract from absorbing cholesterol [N3-F2]. Foods high in soluble fiber include whole-grain cereals, fruits, and legumes [N3-F2]. MedlinePlus also recommends increasing plant stanols and sterols to 2 grams per day, as they also help reduce cholesterol absorption [N3-F2]. These can be found in whole grains, nuts, legumes, oils, and fortified foods [N3-F2].

Omega-3 fatty acids are another key dietary change. MedlinePlus states they can lower LDL and triglyceride levels and may help control blood pressure and reduce heart rhythm problems [N3-F2]. Omega-3 sources include fish such as salmon, tuna, and mackerel, plant sources like walnuts, flaxseed, chia seeds, and canola and soybean oils, and fortified foods [N3-F2]. MedlinePlus also advises limiting cholesterol intake to less than 200 mg per day and limiting salt to no more than 2,300 milligrams per day, because limiting salt lowers blood pressure but not cholesterol directly [N3-F2]. It also notes that alcohol adds extra calories and can lead to weight gain, which raises LDL and lowers HDL [N3-F2].

### Exercise and weight management recommendations

The CDC’s prevention page says eating foods naturally high in fiber and unsaturated fats is part of a heart-healthy approach [N3-R4]. MedlinePlus explicitly states that heart-healthy lifestyle changes include healthy eating, weight management, and regular physical activity [N3-F2]. The CDC also says that cholesterol management should be based on lifetime cardiovascular risk [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that managing weight is part of a broader lifestyle strategy to reduce risk.

### Smoking, alcohol, and other lifestyle factors

The NHS and MedlinePlus both highlight that smoking and drinking alcohol are risk factors [N1-F1][N3-F2]. MedlinePlus specifically says smoking and drinking alcohol are part of the lifestyle factors that can increase risk, and it advises limiting alcohol because it can raise blood pressure and triglyceride levels [N3-F2]. It also says it’s best not to drink, but if someone does drink, men should have no more than 2 drinks per day and women no more than 1 per day [N3-F2]. This makes smoking and alcohol use clear lifestyle issues that should be avoided or reduced.

The CDC’s prevention page also mentions that a sedentary lifestyle and unhealthy diet are important risk factors [N1-R2], reinforcing that regular physical activity is central to managing cholesterol [N3-F2]. Together, the evidence suggests a clear daily management plan: eat more fiber and healthy fats, limit saturated and trans fats and cholesterol, include omega-3s, control alcohol and smoking, and keep weight and physical activity in check [N3-F2][N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-R1].

## 6. Practical next steps and when to seek more help

### What to do after a cholesterol test

The CDC says the only way to know whether you have high cholesterol is to get your cholesterol checked, and that the cholesterol test is a simple blood draw [N4-F3]. It also explains that some cholesterol tests do not require fasting, so patients should follow their healthcare professional’s instructions [N4-R1]. After the test, the CDC notes that repeat tests may be done every 3 to 12 months after the first test to ensure cholesterol levels remain healthy [N4-R3]. The CDC also says that cholesterol should be checked starting early in life, including in children and adolescents, and that people with heart disease, diabetes, or a family history of high cholesterol need to be tested more often [N4-F3].

The CDC further says that your healthcare team will look at cholesterol numbers alongside family history, age, sex, smoking, and other health factors to assess risk [N4-F3]. This means the next step after a test is not just to receive a number, but to discuss the result in context with a healthcare provider. The CDC also says that cholesterol management and treatment decisions should be made in collaboration with a healthcare professional [N4-F3]. This is important because cholesterol levels alone do not tell the whole story.

### When to see a doctor or specialist

The CDC states that people with heart disease, diabetes, or a family history of high cholesterol need more frequent cholesterol checks [N4-F3]. It also says that if cholesterol levels are high, your healthcare team may order a coronary artery calcium (CAC) scan to help understand risk and determine the best way to manage cholesterol levels [N4-F3]. This suggests seeing a doctor if results are abnormal or if the patient has known risk factors. The CDC also notes that children and adolescents should be tested at specific ages, so parents should follow the recommended screening schedule [N4-F3]. In addition, the CDC emphasizes that cholesterol management should be based on lifetime cardiovascular risk, which means people with comorbidities, high blood pressure, or other risk factors should be reviewed more closely [N4-F3].

### How to track progress and stay motivated

The CDC says repeat tests may be done every 3 to 12 months after the first test to check whether levels remain healthy [N4-R3]. This gives a concrete way to track progress over time. MedlinePlus notes that heart-healthy lifestyle changes include healthy eating, weight management, and regular physical activity, and that the main treatments are lifestyle changes and medicines [N3-F2]. This means tracking progress involves both lifestyle adherence and regular blood checks. The CDC also says that cholesterol management should be made in collaboration with a healthcare professional [N4-F3], so staying motivated can be supported by regular follow-up appointments and clear communication with the provider.

Overall, the practical next steps are: get a blood test, follow the healthcare provider’s preparation and fasting instructions, discuss results in context, repeat testing as needed, and work with a healthcare team to decide on lifestyle and treatment changes [N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R3]. If results are concerning or if the patient has known risk factors, seeing a doctor or specialist is important [N4-F3].

## 7. Special considerations for people with other health conditions

### How diabetes, heart failure, kidney disease, and pregnancy affect cholesterol

The evidence shows that cholesterol is part of a broader cardiovascular risk picture. The CDC says cholesterol should be checked starting early in life, and management should be based on lifetime cardiovascular risk, including comorbidities [N4-F3]. This means that people with other conditions need their cholesterol assessed in context, not in isolation. The CDC also says that cholesterol management and treatment decisions should be made in collaboration with a healthcare professional [N4-F3].

The N5 search results show that pregnancy can be especially concerning. The CDC-linked excerpt on cardiovascular complications of pregnancy notes that women with a history of hypertension during pregnancy had higher body mass index, systolic blood pressure, LDL levels, and fasting glucose [N5-R1]. The CardioSmart article says gestational diabetes can damage organs and may be linked to future heart problems [N5-R2]. A Harvard Health article notes that women who experience certain pregnancy complications face higher long-term cardiovascular disease risk [N5-R3]. The Preeclampsia Foundation says women who have had preeclampsia have three to four times the risk of high blood pressure and double the risk for heart disease and stroke [N5-R5]. This shows that pregnancy and related complications can raise cholesterol and other cardiovascular risk factors, even if the patient is not aware of high cholesterol at the time.

### Whether treatment targets differ for special populations

The evidence supports the idea that treatment targets differ. The CDC says cholesterol should be checked more often in people with heart disease, diabetes, or a family history of high cholesterol [N4-F3]. The 2018 cholesterol guidelines emphasize that management should be based on lifetime cardiovascular risk, including age, diabetes, and other factors [N4-F3]. This suggests that people with diabetes or other comorbidities may need earlier or more frequent testing. The evidence also supports using ezetimibe as the preferred initial add-on for very high-risk patients with ASCVD and LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL after maximal statin therapy [N2-R3], showing that treatment intensity can increase in high-risk groups [N2-R3].

### Warnings about medications in vulnerable groups

The evidence does not provide detailed safety profiles for every medication in every vulnerable group, but it does give enough context to infer caution. The CDC says cholesterol management and treatment decisions should be made in collaboration with a healthcare professional [N4-F3], which implies that vulnerable groups are not treated the same way as average patients. The evidence also highlights that PCSK9 inhibitors are used in addition to statins, but that administration every two weeks can be logistically challenging [N2-R2], suggesting that these drugs may not be ideal for all patients.

For pregnancy, the evidence is especially important because high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes are all linked to increased heart disease risk in women [N5-R4]. The CDC-linked excerpt on pregnancy complications notes higher LDL levels in women with hypertension during pregnancy [N5-R1], and the Harvard Health article links pregnancy complications to higher long-term cardiovascular disease risk [N5-R3]. This means women with pregnancy complications should be monitored carefully and treated with caution, especially because pregnancy itself can alter lipid levels and long-term risk [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

## 8. Summary for the patient

If you have “cholestérol élevé” (high cholesterol), here is what you should know:

- **What it means:** You have too much cholesterol in your blood, which can build up in arteries and increase the risk of heart attack and stroke [N1-F1].
- **Why it matters:** It is often silent, so the only reliable way to know is through a blood test [N4-F3].
- **Common causes and risk factors:** Age, sex, family history, eating fatty food, not exercising enough, being overweight, smoking, and drinking alcohol [N1-F1][N1-R2].
- **How it is measured:** A simple blood test called a lipid profile checks LDL, HDL, triglycerides, and total cholesterol [N4-F3].
- **Treatment:** Usually start with statins, then add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors if needed, especially in high-risk patients [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].
- **Lifestyle changes:** Eat more fiber and healthy fats, limit saturated and trans fats, include omega-3s, control alcohol and smoking, and stay physically active [N3-F2][N3-R4].
- **Next steps:** Get a blood test, follow your provider’s instructions, repeat testing as needed, and work with a healthcare professional [N4-F3][N4-R1][N4-R3].
- **Special considerations:** People with diabetes, heart failure, kidney disease, or pregnancy-related conditions may need more frequent testing and tailored management [N4-F3][N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

In short, high cholesterol is a manageable condition, but it requires a combination of blood testing, lifestyle changes, and, if needed, medication [N1-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3]. If you have any other health conditions or are pregnant, it is especially important to work closely with your doctor [N5-R1][N5-R5].
